title: Sikhs in public life abroad
hookLine: Sikhs now serve in parliaments, courts and city halls in many countries

lines: A COUNCIL CHAMBER ON A WEEKNIGHT.
cards: Potholes. That's tonight's business in a half-empty council chamber. A resident at the microphone is complaining about the ones on her street, and she's not wrong.

She lives at the far edge of his ward, and she has never voted for the councilor behind the long desk, the one in the navy turban. He takes notes, asks two practical questions, and promises to send someone out on Monday.
In parliaments, courtrooms and city halls far from Punjab, scenes like this happen with a turban at the desk. Today: Sikhs in public life abroad.

teach.b: First, the road out. This path has followed Sikhs leaving Punjab: as soldiers, farm workers, students, families starting again.
In the countries where they settled, their children and grandchildren grew up as citizens, and some of them stood for office.
Today Sikhs serve as lawmakers, judges, mayors, police officers and city staff in a number of countries. Second, the visible faith.
Some of them keep the turban and the articles of faith at work. Where a turban was unfamiliar, it became something people saw at the judge's bench and in the debating chamber. Third, the root.
In Sorath, at Ang 671 of the Guru Granth Sahib, Guru Arjan says: I have made everyone my friend, and I am a friend to all.
And the Ardas, the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, ends by asking for sarbat da bhala: the good of all. Not the good of Sikhs. The good of all.
For a Sikh at a council desk, that's a working brief. Fourth, the test.

An elected Sikh speaks for everyone in the district: people of every faith and of none, people who agree and people who never will. The resident at the far edge of the ward, who didn't vote for him, is still his to serve.
The pothole on her street is part of the job.

how: Sikhs in many countries serve in elected office, the courts, the police and public services, often keeping the turban and articles of faith; every Ardas ends by asking for sarbat da bhala, the good of all.

o: the morning hymn read at random from the Granth
a Sikh oath of office taken by elected officials
the prayer closing Sikh gatherings, asking the good of all

games.q: public life and the root — tap the pairs.
p: the prayer that closes Sikh gatherings
the pothole on a stranger's street

s: sarbat da bhala asks for the good of Sikhs only
it asks for the good of all.
at Ang 671, Guru Arjan says he has made everyone his friend
he says he has made everyone his friend, and he is a friend to all.
no Sikh abroad has held public office wearing a turban
some have kept the turban and the articles of faith at the desk and on the bench.

games.q: you're a Sikh councilor, and a resident at the far edge of your ward complains about her street. she isn't from your community. what does the tradition point you toward?
o: tell her to find her own representative.
take notes and send someone out, for the good of all.
promise to look at it someday.
games.why: sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and Ang 671's friend to all make a stranger's pothole part of the job.

practice: Breathe out a wish for the good of the people under your own roof, then widen it with each breath: your street, the neighbors you know and the ones you don't, your town, the people who disagree with you, people across a border you'll never meet.
If you pray, you can rest on sarbat da bhala, the good of all, or on Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Ardas. The prayer that closes Sikh gatherings, asking for the good of all, the working brief for Sikh lawmakers, judges and mayors serving far from Punjab. Today's word.

orig.note: sarbat da bhala, the good of all: the last words asked for in the Ardas.

carryVoice: Your line: serving everywhere. The good of all reaches the far edge of the ward. That's today, done.
